# Sponsor / brand / podcast-meta stoplist
#
# Purpose: the contamination dropout probe (nlp/contamination_dropout_probe.py)
# found that ad-sponsor + podcast-meta + Spanish-ad topics are LOAD-BEARING
# for the ideology R^2 (dropping them post hoc moved R2 from 0.451 to 0.395),
# consistent with an advertising-economics confound: which sponsors/networks
# a show carries correlates with its audience's ideology, independent of the
# show's actual political content. This list removes the ad-READ content
# itself (brand names, ad-structural phrases, outro boilerplate) so the
# refit isn't learning "which ads run on this show" as a proxy for ideology.
#
# PRECISION RULE (see nlp/build_sponsor_stoplist.py validation output):
# brand names and ad-structural phrases ONLY. Product CATEGORIES that are
# also legitimate political subjects (gold, bitcoin, crypto, insurance,
# health) are deliberately NOT here -- removing them would strip real
# content, not just the ad copy wrapped around it.
#
# Two kinds of entries:
#   - lines with no spaces: single tokens, added to the stopword-removal
#     set during tokenization (same mechanism as spoken_stopwords.txt).
#   - lines with spaces: multi-word phrases, removed from the RAW TEXT via
#     case-insensitive substring match BEFORE tokenization (so "use code"
#     doesn't survive as separate "use" + "code" tokens after stopword
#     removal drops "use" but leaves "code" clustering with the next brand
#     name).
#
# Every entry below was frequency-validated against the full 40,242-passage
# corpus before inclusion (see nlp/build_sponsor_stoplist.py) -- included
# only if its usage was overwhelmingly ad-context, not incidental.

# ---- brand names (single token, validated low-collision) ----
quince
shopify
kalshi
duracell
clorox
seafoam
groons
nbc

# ---- brand names (multi-word phrase, single-word form too ambiguous) ----
mint mobile
delta air

# ---- ad-structural phrases ----
.com slash
dot com slash
promo code
use code
brought to you by
this episode is sponsored
sponsored by
for a limited time
terms apply
terms and conditions apply
free shipping
percent off
% off

# ---- podcast-meta / outro phrases ----
thanks for listening
rate and review
leave a review
new episodes every
wherever you get your podcasts
link in the description
hit subscribe
today's episode is brought to you

# ============================================================
# BORDERLINE -- CONSIDERED AND EXCLUDED (documented, not applied)
# ============================================================
# Each of these appeared in a hand-flagged ad/meta topic's top-10 words but
# failed the frequency/collision validation below. Listed here so the
# exclusion is auditable, not silent.
#
#   lincoln       -- 957 hits (2.4% of passages), but "lincoln financial"
#                    (the actual sponsor phrase) appears only ONCE. The
#                    overwhelming majority of "lincoln" mentions are almost
#                    certainly Abraham Lincoln or THE LINCOLN PROJECT (a
#                    real anti-Trump political organization) -- stoplisting
#                    this would have been a serious false positive.
#   delta         -- 314 hits (0.8%) bare vs. 109 for "delta air" specifically;
#                    most "delta" mentions are not the airline sponsor
#                    (COVID Delta variant, "delta" as change, etc.). Used
#                    the phrase "delta air" instead of the bare token.
#   yorker        -- 912 hits (2.3%) bare vs. 9 for "new yorker magazine".
#                    "The New Yorker" is a legitimate media outlet that gets
#                    discussed as CONTENT (its journalism, its writers), not
#                    just advertised -- too content-adjacent to stoplist.
#   monarch       -- 461 hits (1.1%) bare vs. 0 for "monarch money" (the
#                    sponsor's actual name never appears verbatim) --
#                    whatever "monarch" is being used for in this corpus,
#                    it isn't reliably the sponsor.
#   tom           -- 29.5% of passages contain "tom" as a substring --
#                    absurdly overbroad (common first name incl. real
#                    political figures, e.g. Sen. Tom Cotton).
#   atlanta       -- 1.3% of passages; a real US city with real political
#                    content (elections, state politics). Not stoplisted.
#   georgia       -- 4.3% of passages; a real US state with heavy genuine
#                    political content (Senate races, 2020/2024 election
#                    disputes). Not stoplisted.
#   armstrong,    -- generic surnames (podcast co-host/guest names on some
#   getty, buck,     shows) that risk colliding with real political figures
#   peter            (e.g. "Buck" = Buck Sexton, a real conservative host).
#                    Left unaddressed by this stoplist; if these persist as
#                    their own topics after refitting, that's a sign of a
#                    genuine show-specific-banter topic, not solvable by a
#                    brand stoplist without over-reach.
#   go to         -- 31.9% of passages ("go to war", "go to the polls", ...).
#                    Far too generic despite also appearing in ad reads
#                    ("go to quince.com").
#   check out     -- 3.4% of passages, same over-broad problem.
#   subscribe     -- 7.4% of passages bare; kept only in the anchored phrase
#                    "hit subscribe" rather than as a standalone token.
#   according to  -- appears constitutively in news-wire-quote-boilerplate
#                    topics (e.g. moderate regime's T45) but is also
#                    extremely common in ordinary substantive reporting
#                    ("according to the CBO...", "according to the poll...").
#                    Removing it corpus-wide would strip real content far
#                    more than it strips boilerplate. T45-style topics are
#                    expected to persist after cleaning as a known,
#                    documented limitation -- not solvable by vocabulary
#                    removal without unacceptable collateral damage.
